questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14226644/assets/f0faa92e0f89c86248abffad7f61cac5d94a3848a7f7be4464c4b28d3915aa32.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{5}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[{5}^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (5\sqrt{5}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z=xy$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=xy,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14226644/assets/f0faa92e0f89c86248abffad7f61cac5d94a3848a7f7be4464c4b28d3915aa32.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)=x,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(y)^{2}+(x)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}r\sqrt{1+{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot {[\frac{2}{3}\,{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}[{2}^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{2\pi (2\sqrt{2}-1)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14226644/assets/f6200343142274ee2f5b3934cbe014ee24edf8177f3a544c38dc070bb7df83ef.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=2\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{cos}^{2}⁡x+8}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{9(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{cos}^{2}⁡x,$ we get $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{\pi }{2} \\ u & 2 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{2}^{1}\sqrt{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2({2}^{3/2}-1) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\sqrt{1+4x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{1+4x}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14226644/assets/9a459a9807befc312528771626dca293a7ebbccd97a2c1e938f47a2d90a36726.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3})=2\sqrt{x}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}{3})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(2\sqrt{x})}^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1+4x}}\sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+4x}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{1+4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+4x}\cdot \sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(1+4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x+2{x}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(2+8)-0 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z}$ that lies inside the elliptical cylinder $\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}=1.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z},\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})=3{y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})={e}^{z},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2})}^{2}+({e}^{z})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,$ and $\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.$
